description: We are junior undergraduates collaborating to turn fresh ideas into impactful, real world solutions. Our shared focus is to build an ambitious project while deepening our technical skills and teamwork
summary: StellarEye is a web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to help users investigate objects in the sky using real telescope data, with the search for Planet X as its starting point. It allows users to explore sky regions, view optical and infrared images, and access SPHEREx observations through NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive. Its Candidate Finder identifies bright spots, while Object Explorer checks nearby astronomical catalogues through SIMBAD. Users can also explore observation timelines, compare images, examine different wavelengths, and save candidate coordinates for later investigation. The application includes four saved observations around WISE 0855 for demonstration. It was developed using React, FastAPI, and Astropy to process FITS files and sky coordinates. StellarEye also provides explanations and astronomy resources to help users understand telescope data and investigate potential objects before drawing conclusions.
details:
We built StellarEye for the NASA Space Apps Challenge because we wanted to make it easier to investigate what’s in a patch of sky using real telescope data. The search for Planet X gave us a starting question. If something faint catches your eye in an infrared image, how do you find out what you’re looking at? You need to know which observations cover that area, what was already catalogued there, and whether the spot shows up in another image. We brought those steps together in one web app.

In Sky Explorer, you can type an object name or enter its sky coordinates directly. You can navigate the sky in Aladin Lite, switch between the DSS2 optical and 2MASS infrared backgrounds, and overlay nearby Gaia DR3 sources for context. Once you choose a search radius, StellarEye asks NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx observations covering that area. You can see when each observation was taken, open a cutout of the region, and follow the link to the original FITS file.

Once you open an image, Candidate Finder marks bright spots that stand out from the background. Clicking a spot opens Object Explorer, which converts its position in the image to sky coordinates and checks SIMBAD for nearby catalog entries. It shows how far away each possible match is, so you can decide what merits a closer look. You can also save the coordinates and come back to the region later, even if the catalog lookup is unavailable.

The Timeline puts the observations in date order. In Time Comparison, you can line up two images of the same region and view them side by side, overlay them, or switch rapidly between them using Blink. Spectral Explorer shows which wavelengths the observations cover and lets you sample brightness at the position you’re investigating. We included four saved SPHEREx observations from the region around WISE 0855, a cold brown dwarf, so users can try the workflow even if the live archive is unavailable. The demo’s Blink pair was taken at different central wavelengths, so an apparent change can come from the wavelength as well as the time of observation.

We built the interface in React, with a FastAPI backend and Astropy for reading FITS files and working with sky coordinates. We also added short explanations beside unfamiliar terms and a Learn tab with sourced astronomy facts. We wanted someone opening a FITS image for the first time to be able to find a source, see where the data came from, and understand what they would need to check before drawing a conclusion.
